profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting for an internal tool called ArchScope, which uses multi-objective search to reconstruct candidate software architectures from a large legacy enterprise codebase. A prototype design has already been circulated, and this meeting is to decide whether the current design is ready for the next milestone: an internal pilot with the architecture review board using the Atlas system as the first target. The agenda is to review the proposed evaluation flow, what it means to evaluate candidate architectures, whether the algorithm runs will be comparable enough for board-facing review, what input is assumed by 'the standard Atlas baseline,' and what functionality is implied by supporting a nightly run. The expected outcome is conditional approval of the design with a few documented follow-ups, even though the two participants quietly leave with different understandings of what exactly the approved workflow includes.

members.name: Priya Raman
members.expertise: Legacy modernization, architecture recovery, modularization strategy, architecture governance
members.background: Priya has spent more than a decade leading modernization programs for large enterprise platforms and now sponsors ArchScope as a decision-support tool for architects working on eroded legacy systems.
members.private_state: She wants the design review to end with approval so the pilot stays on schedule, but she is quietly concerned that the proposal still behaves more like a research benchmark than something architects can actually review in their normal governance workflow.
hidden_assumptions: When people say they will 'evaluate candidate architectures,' they mean architects will inspect rendered, high-level views and compare trade-offs in a board-friendly format.

A 'candidate architecture' is only candidate-ready once low-level clustering has already been transformed into recognizable architectural slices that a human reviewer can interpret without extra analyst work.

If runs are described as 'comparable,' then they must be comparable under the same review conditions, including aligned compute budgets, similarly shaped outputs, and normalized trade-off presentation.
The phrase 'the standard Atlas baseline' refers to the architecture team's usual baseline artifact, because that is the obvious default input for any review meant for architects.
A 'nightly run' for a pilot means the entire overnight workflow finishes in a morning-ready state, not merely that the search job has started or persisted intermediate artifacts.

members.name: Lukas Meyer
members.expertise: Search-based software engineering, evolutionary multi-objective optimization, experiment infrastructure, evaluation automation
members.background: Lukas joined from a research lab focused on SBSE tooling and now owns the optimization engine and evaluation pipeline behind ArchScope.
members.private_state: He wants approval for a design that preserves experimental rigor and implementation simplicity, and he is trying to avoid prematurely committing the team to expensive visualization and packaging work before the optimization core is validated.
hidden_assumptions: When people say they will 'evaluate candidate architectures,' they mean the harness will score and compare optimization outputs using objective metrics over the generated Pareto front.
A 'candidate architecture' can still be a raw optimization result, such as a module-to-cluster assignment, as long as it is valid input for downstream analysis or later visualization.

If runs are described as 'comparable,' then each algorithm only needs to be evaluated under a defensible setup consistent with accepted SBSE practice, even if runtime budgets and archive behavior differ.

The phrase 'the standard Atlas baseline' refers to the baseline already standardized in the automated pipeline, because reproducibility depends on using the shared extraction everyone runs by default.

A 'nightly run' means the automated batch search executes overnight and stores results; any curation, ranking interpretation, or presentation assembly can happen afterward without violating that label.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to evaluate candidate architectures
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss 'evaluating candidate architectures' and agree that this is what the pilot and the design should support.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means human architects evaluating architect-facing reconstructed views, such as diagrams or organized comparison screens that present high-level architectural alternatives.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the evaluation harness computing objective scores and comparing raw search outputs across Pareto fronts, whether or not those outputs are yet in a human-friendly architectural form.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is standard in architecture-recovery work and naturally blends human review with quantitative assessment, so both can use it fluently without realizing they are pointing to different stages of the workflow.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree the algorithms need to be 'comparable' in the evaluation harness.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes comparability means fair side-by-side review conditions for decision-making, including equivalent computational budget, similarly constrained outputs, and trade-off views that can be interpreted consistently by architects.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes comparability means each algorithm is configured in a technically respectable way according to its own method family, even if one runs longer, produces a different number of non-dominated solutions, or uses a different archive policy.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Comparable is a high-status term that signals rigor to both research and engineering audiences, so each participant hears confirmation of their own standard and has little reason to probe further in a cooperative review.

misalignment_points.topic: Which artifact 'the standard Atlas baseline' refers to
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to validating the design on 'the standard Atlas baseline.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the architecture team's usual review baseline for Atlas: the preprocessed structural view they routinely use when discussing subsystem boundaries and erosion with architects.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the pipeline's usual Atlas baseline: the automatically extracted repository snapshot already wired into the search and evaluation infrastructure.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Internally, both artifacts are routinely called the standard Atlas baseline, and because neither participant expects there to be another plausible object behind that label, the shared name creates strong false consensus.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in a nightly run
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the design should support a 'nightly run' before the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the nightly run includes whatever is necessary for the next morning's review activity: extraction, optimization, post-processing, ranking, and production of an architect-consumable comparison bundle.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the nightly run includes only the automated ingestion and search pipeline up to persisted results, with interpretation and presentation steps occurring later as separate activities.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Nightly run is common shorthand for an overnight batch capability, and both participants reasonably treat their own boundary as the obvious one, so the phrase feels precise enough even though it silently hides different endpoints.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to end in approval, but I still need a little signal that we're not taking a research-style prototype into a board setting. When I say evaluate candidate architectures, I'm thinking of the review board looking at reconstructed, recognizable architecture views in their usual governance format. And for Atlas, the obvious starting point is the standard Atlas baseline the architects already use in subsystem and erosion discussions.
turns.utterance: Thanks, Lukas. I'd like to use this review to settle whether ArchScope is ready for the Atlas pilot and whether the current design supports evaluating candidate architectures in the board's normal flow. I also want to make sure we're validating on the standard Atlas baseline before we call the milestone closed.

turns.inner_thought: That's a framing I can work with. The design is ready if we keep the commitment around the harness: run the optimization variants on the standard Atlas baseline already wired into the pipeline, then evaluate candidate architectures across the objective trade-offs. I should keep this centered on the core search and evaluation path, not invite premature promises on packaging.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's how I've been framing it too. The proposal is essentially an evaluation harness that runs the main multi-objective variants on the standard Atlas baseline and then evaluates candidate architectures across the trade-offs they produce. From my side, that's the core capability we need for the pilot.

turns.inner_thought: So far this still sounds compatible, but I need to test usability without forcing him into a corner. If the board is going to evaluate candidate architectures, they need something they can review directly, not raw cluster assignments that still need analyst interpretation. I need him to reassure me while letting this stay on track.
turns.utterance: That sounds reasonable. My practical question is whether, in the pilot, the outputs will be in a shape the board can work with directly when they evaluate candidate architectures, rather than us having to do a lot of bridging around the process.

turns.inner_thought: She wants confidence that the results are usable, which is fair. For me they're fully evaluable once the harness scores the Pareto outputs and exposes the trade-off space in a consistent way; any presentation layer can sit on top of that same path later. I should answer cleanly and not open a debate about bespoke board-facing views.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's the intent. The candidates will be fully evaluable, and the flow is designed so the trade-off space comes through cleanly rather than us maintaining separate paths for analysis and presentation.

turns.inner_thought: All right, I'm not going to press harder there. The next risk is fairness. When the board compares alternatives, comparable has to mean the methods are being judged under the same review conditions, not just that each one was run however its owner prefers. But I'll keep that concern at the surface level so we don't derail approval.
turns.utterance: Okay. Then the main approval question for me is confidence that the different search methods will be comparable when the board looks across alternatives. If we're putting more than one approach in front of them, I want that comparison to hold together.

turns.inner_thought: Absolutely, they need to be comparable in a rigorous evaluation sense. That means each method is set up in a defensible way for its family so the comparison is respectable and reproducible, not flattened into arbitrary symmetry. I need to sound reassuring without getting dragged into equal-budget commitments.
turns.utterance: I agree. The design assumes the methods will be comparable in the harness, and I'll keep the setup disciplined enough that the comparison is technically solid rather than ad hoc.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll reinforce Atlas as a familiar anchor. In my mind that's the review baseline the architecture group already knows, so it should help the board read the outputs without additional translation. If he agrees, that's enough for today.
turns.utterance: Good. I also think using the standard Atlas baseline helps, because it's already the reference point people are used to when they talk about erosion and subsystem boundaries. That should lower the friction for the pilot.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, exactly—though I'm thinking of the automated baseline already standardized in the pipeline. Reusing it keeps the path reproducible and means I don't have to support a separate preparation workflow for this one milestone. Best to confirm in general terms.
turns.utterance: I agree. Reusing that baseline is the cleanest option because it keeps the run path stable and avoids creating a special preparation track just for Atlas.

turns.inner_thought: Now I need to cover operations. For me, nightly run means the entire overnight workflow finishes in a morning-ready state: extraction, search, post-processing, ranking, and a comparison bundle the architects can open. I can't say all that without reopening scope, so I'll phrase it in the way any architect would take for granted.
turns.utterance: The other thing I'd like us to treat as part of pilot readiness is a nightly run. Operationally, that should leave everything ready for the morning review so the architects aren't depending on extra setup before they start.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine—I can agree with that wording. For me, nightly run means the overnight automation executes and stores results so the morning starts from completed batch output, not a manual restart. I do not want to commit the batch contract to every downstream curation step, but I don't need to say that here.
turns.utterance: Yes, agreed. The nightly run should be automatic and reliable, with the overnight path leaving things ready so the morning review can proceed without babysitting the process.

turns.inner_thought: That is enough to approve without forcing every hidden boundary into the open. I'll condition approval on interpretability, Atlas as the baseline, and comparable methods. If the first pilot output doesn't look board-ready, I'll have room to tighten expectations later.
turns.utterance: All right. I'm comfortable approving the design on that basis, provided evaluating candidate architectures on the standard Atlas baseline stays interpretable and the algorithms remain comparable. With those conditions, I think we're in good shape for the internal pilot.

turns.inner_thought: Great. Approval, and still no hard commitment to expensive visualization work up front. I'll document comparability in the SBSE sense, wire the existing Atlas baseline through the milestone path, and define nightly run around the automated batch behavior. From my perspective, that's exactly the right scope.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll move ahead with implementation and document the comparable evaluation setup, the Atlas baseline integration, and the nightly run behavior in the milestone notes so we have a clear path into the pilot.
